Flying on Mars

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
... they are sending a helicopter to fly on Mars

Unique Selling Point:
New otherwordly technology

Summary:
A new vehicle -- a small helicopter will be sent to Mars in August to fly in the thin atmosphere. And it is the brain child of a Namibian -- Dr Japie van Zyl.

Further information:
On the first of August 2020 Nasa will launch its next Mars mission. It is sending a new rover to Mars, called Perseverance) that will not only explore the surface but also, bore into the surface of Mars and collect samples that will be brought back to Earth by future missions.

But fixed under the Ingenuity Rover something new and very revolutionary is hitching a ride to the Martian surface. It will be deployed once the rover reaches the Martian surface in 2021

This hitchhiker is a small drone helicopter and will be the first human-made object to fly in the thin Martian air. It is experimental technology and is planned to be used to test the technology to scout interesting targets on Mars and help plan the best driving route for future Mars rovers.

Built to be light and strong enough to stow away under the rover while on the way to Mars, and survive the harsh Martian environment after arriving on the surface. The helicopter weighs less than 4 pounds (1.8 kilograms).
It is powerful enough to lift off in the thin Mars atmosphere. The atmosphere of Mars is very thin: less than 1% the density of Earth's.

It is expected to fly up to five times during its 30-day test campaign, early in the rover's mission, as it is primarily a technology demonstration.

Each flight is planned to take no more than three minutes, at altitudes ranging from 3 to 10 m above the ground. It could potentially cover a distance of up to 300 metres (980 ft) per flight. It can use autonomous control and communicate with the Perseverance rover directly after each landing.

If it works as expected, NASA could build on the design for future Mars aerial missions.

The person who is principally responsible for the development of the helicopter is a Southern African engineer from Namibia who studied at the University of Stellenbosch.

Until very recently he was the Director of Solar System Exploration at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California and has been with Nasa for 33 years. He has received an honorary doctorate form Stellenbosch University and is seen as one of the most influential people in space exploration in the world.

His name is Japie van Zyl, also known as Jacob van Zyl in the US. The helicopter is his baby, and while he recently left Nasa, he is still working with the project leader who took over from him, MiMi Aung.

The story is about the absolutely ground-breaking project and the technology that will be employed for the first time on another planet. And it has a South African link through Japie.

Treatment

Both Japie and MiMi are prepared to speak to us and have unique photographs and footage of the helicopter while it was being built and test flights. Nasa also has high-end animations showing how the helicopter will fly on Mars.

We will also use a South African Expert on Mars form the Astronomical Association of South Africa -- Clyde Foster. He has a powerful telescope at his home focused on Mars and he is an expert photographer of Mars.

We will start the insert with the presenter looking through a telescope at Mars and showing some of Clyde's photographs of Mars, and then introduce the extraordinary event that will take place -- an Earth helicopter that will soon fly on the red planet. This first in human history.

We will briefly recap why Mars is so important now with so many missions to Mars are taking place right now -- eg both the UAE and Russian have launched probes to Mars in the last 10 days.

Then we will get to Nasa Mission that has launched successfully on 30 July and we have great footage of the launch and give more detail on the helicopter called Ingenuity (eg it was named by high school students), and what it can and will do.

There is a lot of visuals available:
Clyde's photographs of Mars from Earth
All the launches
Stunning photographs of the Martian surface that have been taken by the Curiosity Rover
Great material on the building of the Rover and Helicopter and test flights
Great animations of the new Perseverance rover and what it will do on Mars
Great animations of the helicopter flying on Mars


Expert:
Dr. Japie van Zyl
Dr. MiMi Aung
Mr. Clyde Foster

Script:


V/O:
The past few weeks have been really exciting in the field of space exploration. In a first, a private company taxied astronauts to the international space station and brought back two others. The splashdown of their capsule was the first by American astronauts in 45 years.

But all of this pales in comparison to the excitement that accompanied this rocket that blasted off to Mars on the 30th of July.
18



10
LINK:
It seems that there is currently unprecedented interest in the Red Planet. As we speak there are three rockets on their way to Mars.
V/O:
Both China and the United Arab Emirates have also launched missions to Mars the last three weeks.

Dr Japie van Zyl, a Namibian who studied in Stellenbosch, was until recently the Director for Solar System Exploration at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

We first met him a decade and a half ago when the Opportunity rover was deployed on Mars. Over the years he has received many honours, including an honorary doctorate from Stellenbosch University.

He was deeply involved with the NASA launch to Mars and says the current missions will arrive within days of each other -- seven months down the line, the flight time to Mars..
7

10


14


11
Japie:
It is going to be an interesting situation next year. It is almost like the Earth invasion of Mars When the three different missions arrive there all about the same time. …about the planet.
V/O:
The American mission is taking a rover, called Perseverance to Mars to look for signs of past life.

But the actual excitement is about a small machine that will accompany Perseverance. It is a tiny helicopter and is destined to become the first aircraft to fly on another planet.
7

13
Bob:
Ja, I think it is hopefully the start of a new exploration ear for Mars.
V/O:
Dr Bob Balaram is the Chief Engineer on the Mars Helicopter project and has been involved in designing and building the craft. It all started about seven years ago.
12
Bob:
Our director had heard about drones and things and he came back to JPL and said “Can we do this on Mars?”
V/O:
The Director was none other than Dr Japie van Zyl. The team believed that an aircraft could be really helpful to the surface rovers. 10
LINK:
The surface rovers on Mars can only explore where the terrain allows them. An aircraft can explore areas where the rovers cannot reach.
V/O:
And the helicopter can scout ahead for the best route for the rover to take. 6
Japie:
And in fact, this was originally called the Mars Helicopter Scout because of the fact that it was supposed to scout ahead of the rover.
V/O:
Clyde Foster is a world-renowned amateur astronomer. From the observatory at his home he has been photographing Mars, Jupiter and Saturn for years. A few months ago Foster’s work earned him international recognition.
14
LINK:
On the 31st of May this year, Clyde made astronomical history when he discovered something in outer space.
V/O:
That night he was taking photographs of Jupiter through his telescope and used a methane filter. 6
Clyde:
And once I had started imaging with this specific filter I could immediately see that there was a bright spot just below right of the great red spot. Once I had started opening up communication with some of my professional colleagues and the rest of the international community, it pretty much became clear that it was an outbreak. This is basically a plume of gas from Jupiter’s atmosphere that erupts out the upper layers of the atmosphere, almost like a mushroom cloud from a nuclear explosion.
V/O:
Foster was the only person on Earth to observe this short-lived phenomenon, and Nasa named the spot after him – it will forever officially be known as Clyde’s spot. He has also been fascinated with Mars for years.

He says flying on Mars would be a challenge as the Red Planet is an inhospitable place. It is further away from the sun than the Earth, with an average surface temperature of minus 81 degrees Celsius.
17
15


15
Clyde:
It is fascinating to watch it on a day to day basis. You have the weather conditions that you are monitoring, cloud fronts that are forming and de-forming you have the North and South Polar caps that grow and reduce as the season changes.
LINK:
Mars has an atmosphere and you can see the sky, just as you can see it on Earth. However, the Martian atmosphere has only 1% of the density of Earth’s atmosphere.
Japie:
The question I got asked the most about this project was: “Is it even possible to fly in an atmosphere that is as thin as Mars?”
V/O:
To answer this question, they created a simple prototype and tested it in a vacuum chamber, simulating the air pressure on Mars.
9
Japie:
We couldn’t actually control the helicopter that we flew in the chamber. We would just take off and then we would shut off the engine and it would drop back to the floor. So we affectionate called it our little hopper.
V/O:
But it proved that flight on Mars would be possible, especially since gravity on Mars is just 40% of that on Earth.
10
LINK:
Mars is famous for its large, planet-wide dust storms. This one is about 300 X 400 km, with winds of up to 100 km per hour. Surely this poses a serious threat to Ingenuity
V/O:
This is because it the aircraft weighs just under two its blades are over a metre long. 7
Bob:
Unlike the movie “The Martian” where everything blew over when the storms came, a hundred kilometre per hour wind on Mars is the same as a 10 km per hour wind here on earth. Because the density is a hundred times less, the wind effect is so much less.
V/O:
Since the Perseverance rover’s main objective is to look for signs of previous life, the landing site in The Jezero crater was chosen very carefully.
10
Clyde:
It is an amazing site. The crater is about 50 km across, so it is a relatively small crater but the tell-tale signs of water have been pretty clearly indicated there. What is has, it has and inflow stream and also an outflow stream so the indication is that in the distant past there would have been water flowing into the crater, presumably forming a lake, and then overflowing out of the crater.
Japie:
And the instruments we have on board are optimized to look for fossilized life in rocks and so forth. This is taking that next step, we know that Mars could have support life, now the question is: “Did life ever start?”
V/O:
We might have the answer to this early next year, who knows. But it is clear that those who gaze at the stars and try the impossible on a distant planet all subscribe to the same basic philosophy:

Japie:
Do not go where the path may lead. Instead go where there is no path and leave a trail.

The helicopter weighs less than 4 pounds (1.8 kilograms). It is powerful enough to lift off in the thin Mars atmosphere. The atmosphere of Mars is very thin: less than 1% the density of Earth's. It is expected to fly up to five times during its 30-day test campaign, early in the rover's mission, as it is primarily a technology demonstration. Each flight is planned to take no more than three minutes, at altitudes ranging from 3 to 10 m above the ground. It could potentially cover a distance of up to 300 metres (980 ft) per flight. It can use autonomous control and communicate with the Perseverance rover directly after each landing. If it works as expected, NASA could build on the design for future Mars aerial missions. The person who is principally responsible for the development of the helicopter is a Southern African engineer from Namibia who studied at the University of Stellenbosch. Until very recently he was the Director of Solar System Exploration at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California and has been with Nasa for 33 years. He has received an honorary doctorate form Stellenbosch University and is seen as one of the most influential people in space exploration in the world. His name is Japie van Zyl, also known as Jacob van Zyl in the US. The helicopter is his baby, and while he recently left Nasa, he is still working with the project leader who took over from him, MiMi Aung. The story is about the absolutely ground-breaking project and the technology that will be employed for the first time on another planet. And it has a South African link through Japie. Treatment Both Japie and MiMi are prepared to speak to us and have unique photographs and footage of the helicopter while it was being built and test flights. Nasa also has high-end animations showing how the helicopter will fly on Mars. We will also use a South African Expert on Mars form the Astronomical Association of South Africa -- Clyde Foster. He has a powerful telescope at his home focused on Mars and he is an expert photographer of Mars. We will start the insert with the presenter looking through a telescope at Mars and showing some of Clyde's photographs of Mars, and then introduce the extraordinary event that will take place -- an Earth helicopter that will soon fly on the red planet. This first in human history. We will briefly recap why Mars is so important now with so many missions to Mars are taking place right now -- eg both the UAE and Russian have launched probes to Mars in the last 10 days. Then we will get to Nasa Mission that has launched successfully on 30 July and we have great footage of the launch and give more detail on the helicopter called Ingenuity (eg it was named by high school students), and what it can and will do. There is a lot of visuals available: Clyde's photographs of Mars from Earth All the launches Stunning photographs of the Martian surface that have been taken by the Curiosity Rover Great material on the building of the Rover and Helicopter and test flights Great animations of the new Perseverance rover and what it will do on Mars Great animations of the helicopter flying on Mars
